title: Concealment is not the same as blinding
task: Work out which protection site 7 has lost
scene: Farida Diouf has a note from site 7. Their pharmacy diary lists kit numbers beside the arm each one contains, and the research nurse can see the next entry before she decides whether to enter a patient.
question: What has site 7's readable diary cost CLARION-3?
takeaway: If the next assignment can be seen in advance, chance is no longer the only thing choosing.
why: Randomisation only buys balanced groups if nobody can see what is coming. A nurse who knows the next slot is the drug can wait a day for a patient she thinks will do well, or enter a frailer one when the next slot is standard care. Neither is dishonest and both destroy the comparison, because the arms now differ in who was entered as well as in what they were given. Concealment protects the moment of entry. Blinding protects everything after it, and the two fail separately.
assumes: participants are assigned to arms by chance rather than by choice

choices: The groups can differ by who was picked, not only by luck
The nurse giving the infusion will be able to tell what is in the bag
Participants at site 7 will work out which arm they are on
The pharmacy can no longer reconcile shipped kit against what was dispensed
rebuttals: That is blinding, and it fails later — after entry, when somebody is treating or measuring.
Participants guessing is a real problem, and it is also after the fact rather than at entry.
Accountability is the pharmacy's own record and is not what the diary has broken.

title: One outcome, named in advance
task: Separate what the trial counts from what it also collects
scene: Kwame Ansah has four measurements from the same participant on his screen and a definition agreed four years ago. A journalist has asked the sponsor which of the four CLARION-3 is actually about.
question: Why does CLARION-3 name one of its outcomes as primary before it starts?
takeaway: The primary endpoint is the one question the trial was built to answer; the rest are collected, not promised.
why: A trial accepts a small chance of calling a difference real when there is none. That budget was set for one comparison. Collect twelve outcomes and read whichever comes out best, and the chance of an impressive-looking result rises with every one, because ordinary variation gets twelve opportunities instead of one. Naming the endpoint in advance is what stops the trial choosing its own question after seeing the answers. The others are still collected, still reported, and carry no such protection.
assumes: a trial collects more than one measurement from each participant

choices: It fixes which comparison the error budget covers
It tells sites which measurement to take most carefully at every visit
It marks the outcome that matters most to participants
It is the outcome the drug was most likely to change
rebuttals: Sites take every trial measurement to protocol; care is not rationed by which one is primary.
Importance to participants is why an endpoint is chosen, not what naming it in advance does.
Being most likely to move is an argument for choosing it, not a reason to fix it beforehand.

title: A trial ends at a number of events
task: Work out what the trial is waiting for
scene: Balogun wants to know when CLARION-3 will be finished and has been told, twice, that nobody can say. Feldman writes three quantities on the whiteboard and asks him to estimate it himself.
question: Estimate how many events CLARION-3 needs before it can answer its question.
takeaway: A trial powered on events finishes when the events arrive, which is not a date.
why: A time-to-event trial learns from events, not from people. Two thousand participants who stay well carry almost no information about which arm is better; the comparison rests on the ones something happened to. So the design fixes a number of events, and recruitment and follow-up run until that number arrives. It is why nobody can promise a completion date, why a healthier-than-expected group is bad news for the schedule, and why the interim looks are placed at fractions of the events rather than at fractions of the years.
assumes: the trial compares how often an event happens in two arms

estimate.prompt: CLARION-3 is powered to detect a hazard ratio of 0.75 with a two-sided 5 per cent test and 80 per cent power. For a 1:1 allocation the required events are 4(z + z)² divided by the square of the log hazard ratio.
estimate.question: Choose the constant, the z term and the log hazard ratio squared.
estimate.relationship: Required events ≈ 4(z + z)² ÷ (ln HR)², with z the two normal cut-offs for the error rate and the power, and HR the hazard ratio the trial is built to detect.
estimate.explanation: About 380 events. CLARION-3 has 246 of them, which is why the second interim is where it is: the board reads the trial at roughly two thirds of the information it will ever have.
givens: The trial is powered for a hazard ratio of 0.75
At 5 per cent two-sided and 80 per cent power, (z + z)² is 7.85
labels: 7.85  ((z + z)² at 5 per cent two-sided and 80 per cent power)

equations.about: how many events a trial has to see to answer its question

title: A number can be precise and still be the wrong outcome
task: Match each measurement to the weakness that can bend what it means.
scene: Kwame Ansah has four CLARION-3 measurements on his table. One comes from a national register, one from blinded readers, one from a treating doctor, and one from a central laboratory. Doyle wants to know what can go wrong with each.
takeaway: Before trusting a number, ask both how it was made and whether it measures the outcome people actually care about.
why: Measurements can fail in different ways. A death in a national register needs little trial judgement. A borderline admission can move if readers apply the definition differently, so blinded adjudication protects it. A symptom score can move with the scorer’s belief about treatment. A laboratory marker can be measured perfectly and still mislead. If it stands in for a clinical outcome, it is a surrogate. Changing the marker does not prove that admissions, symptoms or survival changed with it.
assumes: a measurement can be precise without being clinically important
a surrogate outcome is a measure used to stand in for a clinical outcome

choices: Almost none from trial judgement; the event is recorded outside the study.
A borderline case can move if the definition is applied differently.
The scorer’s belief about treatment can shift a subjective rating.
It can improve even if the clinical outcome it stands in for does not.
scenarios: Death from any cause, taken from the national register.
A hospital admission for the trial condition, ruled on by three blinded readers.
A symptom score the treating doctor writes at each visit.
A blood inflammation marker measured by the central laboratory and used as a stand-in for future admission.

title: What counts as a deviation
task: Decide what a deviation is worth recording
scene: Lucia Marchetti has four things sites did this month that were not what the protocol says. None of them harmed anybody. Site 12 has asked which of them are worth the paperwork.
question: Which of these most threatens the comparison CLARION-3 is making?
takeaway: A deviation is recorded for what it does to the comparison, not for how bad it looks.
why: Deviations matter in proportion to what they do to the two arms. A late blood test and a late form are untidy and affect both arms equally, so the comparison survives them. A different pump delivers the same drug. Entering people the trial was not designed for changes who is in it — and if that site's entries are not spread evenly across the arms, it changes what is being compared. The test is always whether the two groups are still alike apart from the treatment.
assumes: the protocol states what should happen at each visit

choices: A site entered four people who did not qualify
A site took the twelve-week bloods a week late, at thirteen weeks
A site filed its visit forms a fortnight late
A site used a different brand of infusion pump
rebuttals: A week's delay applies to both arms and leaves the comparison intact.
Late paperwork is a data-management problem; the visit itself happened on time.
A different pump is a deviation worth recording and does not alter who is in which arm.

title: The plan that was in force
task: Order what has to be true before an interim analysis can be called prespecified.
scene: Nkechi Umeh has four versions of the analysis plan, each dated. Feldman wants to know which one governs the interim in twenty days, and the sponsor's lawyer wants to know how anybody could prove it.
takeaway: A result is worth more when the plan that produced it can be dated.
why: Prespecification is a claim about time: this analysis was chosen before anybody could see what it would give. The only way to support that claim afterwards is a public record with dates on it, made before the data existed. That is why the plan is registered rather than filed, why the cut comes after the registration rather than before, and why the person who runs it is the one person already permitted to see the arms. Reverse any two of those steps and the analysis is still correct arithmetic about a question chosen after the fact.
assumes: a trial's plan can be amended while it is running

cards: The analysis is written into the plan, with its boundary and its timing.
The plan version is registered publicly, with the date it took effect.
The data are cut at the stated point and the file is locked.
The unblinded statistician runs the analysis that the registered plan names.

title: The clock that is not the analysis clock
task: Decide what moves now, before the next scheduled board meeting can help.
scene: The second admission arrived eighteen minutes ago. One patient is still on the ward, and the two sites are four hundred kilometres apart. Vogt is reachable this afternoon. The next board meeting is nineteen days away.
question: What should happen to these two reports today?
takeaway: A safety report does not wait for the analysis it might belong to.
why: Safety reporting and endpoint analysis run on different clocks. A serious unexpected event may matter to treatment tomorrow, so it cannot wait nineteen days for a board meeting. The site reports what happened now, with enough detail to judge urgency. Whether the event later counts toward a trial endpoint is a separate process. The same event can therefore travel down two paths at once: immediate safety reporting and later blinded adjudication. Waiting for one path to finish before starting the other loses time the safety system was built to protect.
assumes: serious harm during a trial is reported whether or not the drug is thought to have caused it

choices: Both go to the board unblinded now, and recruitment continues
Both wait for the interim pack so the board sees them beside the efficacy result
Recruitment stops today and the reports go with the suspension notice
The sites are asked for more detail and nothing leaves until the files are complete
rebuttals: Holding a safety signal so it arrives with the efficacy result is a scheduling decision, and people are still being infused.
Suspending recruitment is a decision that needs the arms, and nobody blinded can make it.
Complete files are worth having; the report goes now and the detail follows it.

title: Ten minutes on each case
task: Spend the call time on evidence that could change whether the two cases form a pattern.
scene: Lucia Marchetti has ten minutes with each site before the reports go to Vogt. One coordinator is at a bedside. Five useful questions are on her screen, but asking all of them would take longer than either call.
question: What should Marchetti spend the ten minutes finding out before the reports leave?
takeaway: When time is scarce, collect the evidence that can change the decision before collecting detail that only decorates it.
why: Two reports become a signal only when their details line up in a way that could matter. Timing is the fastest discriminator here. A case three days after first exposure tells a different story from one eight months later. Matching intervals in two distant sites would strengthen the case for a shared cause. Different intervals would weaken it. Investigator opinions, recruitment totals and withdrawal status may still matter, but none can establish that temporal pattern before the reports leave.
assumes: a safety pattern depends on whether cases share timing and clinical features
a VALUE board charges time for each piece of evidence
answerText: Buy the exposure timeline first. The dates of first dose, first symptom and admission can show whether the cases share the same exposure clock. Other details can support that judgement, but they cannot replace it.

choices: The dates of first dose, first symptom and admission
The investigator's opinion on whether the drug caused it
The site's recruitment total for the year to date
Whether the participant has been withdrawn from the trial
rebuttals: The investigator's view is collected, but it is an opinion formed without knowing the arm.
Recruitment totals belong to the operations report, not to the case.
Withdrawal is a consequence and can be recorded after the board has read the case.

why_this_format: The old screen asks for one best detail. The instrument makes the player spend a real ten-minute budget and feel the opportunity cost of asking for less decisive information first.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented per-question costs total 15 minutes against the source row's 10-minute budget. The three tempting non-timing items cost 7 minutes; buying them first leaves 3, so the 4-minute exposure timeline can no longer be bought.

data.decision: Do the two admissions share a timing pattern strong enough to flag for the board today?

options.label: Dose, first-symptom and admission dates
options.reveals: Whether both cases began after a similar interval from first exposure.

options.label: New medicines and major lab changes
options.reveals: Whether either case has an obvious competing explanation that weakens the apparent pattern.

options.label: Investigator causality opinion
options.reveals: How each local investigator interprets the case without knowing the treatment arm.

options.label: Site recruitment total this year
options.reveals: How busy each site has been, which does not establish whether these cases share a clinical pattern.

options.label: Whether each participant withdrew
options.reveals: What happened after the admission, not whether the two admissions arose on the same exposure clock.

data.hint: Each question spends the minutes shown beside it. Buy what would most change the pattern decision before using the remaining time on supporting detail.

failure_feedback.action: spending the call on recruitment, withdrawal and causality first
failure_feedback.consequence: seven minutes are gone and the four-minute exposure timeline no longer fits
failure_feedback.line: I can get the rest later. I cannot reconstruct the exposure clock after this call ends.

title: What has to be told, and how fast
task: Match each event to what the trial owes and when.
scene: Umeh has a wall calendar with two windows marked on it in red and a stack of four events from this month. She has to sort them before Friday.
takeaway: Expedited reporting is decided by what the event is, not by what anybody thinks caused it.
why: The reporting window is set by the category, not by the drama. Serious, unexpected and possibly related is the combination that runs on a clock of days, because it is the combination that might change how the drug is used tomorrow. A death nobody thinks is related is still serious and still reported, on the ordinary schedule. An admission for the trial's own condition is the thing being counted, so it goes to adjudication rather than to the safety desk. Everything else lives in the file.
assumes: regulators set deadlines for reporting harm during a trial

choices: Expedited report to the regulator, days rather than weeks.
Recorded as a serious event and reported in the routine safety update.
Recorded as a trial endpoint and adjudicated like any other.
Recorded as an adverse event in the participant's file.
scenarios: An admission with an unexpected liver picture, thought possibly drug-related.
A fatal road accident with no plausible link to the treatment.
A hospital admission for the condition the trial is treating.
A rash that settled in two days without treatment.

title: What an extra look spends
task: Say what a second look costs
scene: The medical director wants one unplanned endpoint summary before noon and has already drafted the email asking for it. Feldman has the two planned looks on the whiteboard and an empty box where this new request would sit.
question: Why does an unplanned look at the endpoint threaten the trial's error rate?
takeaway: A trial's tolerance for error is spent by testing, and it does not refill.
why: A five per cent error rate is a promise about the whole trial, not about one test. Data wander as they accumulate; a difference that looks convincing at one moment can be gone a month later. Each time somebody tests the accumulated data, the trial gets another opportunity to catch that wandering at its most flattering point. Two planned looks are affordable because the boundary at each was made harder to compensate. An unplanned look has no such correction, so it spends error rate the trial never budgeted for.
assumes: a trial accepts a small chance of calling a difference real when there is none

choices: Every look is another chance to cross the line by luck alone
Looking early reduces the number of events the trial will finally collect
The people who see the summary cannot go back to being blinded
An extra analysis has to be repeated after the database is locked
rebuttals: The events keep arriving whether or not anybody looks; looking does not consume them.
Losing the blind is a serious separate harm, and the error rate would rise even if nobody remembered what they saw.
Repeating the analysis later is routine and is not what makes the early look expensive.

equations.about: alpha spending — a budget for error that does not refill

title: Why the board looks and the team does not
task: Decide who is entitled to see what
scene: Vogt is in the building for an hour. Petrescu's closed report is on the table, face down. The medical director is copied on everything the trial team writes and on nothing the board writes.
question: Why is the monitoring board shown the arms when the trial team is not?
takeaway: The people who could act on an early result are the people kept from seeing it.
why: Somebody must see unblinded data or a harmful treatment could continue unnoticed. The safeguard is separation of roles. The monitoring board does not recruit participants, deliver treatment or score outcomes. What it learns cannot change those processes directly. The trial team does all three. If that team knows which arm is winning, ordinary judgement can shift enrolment or follow-up. It can also shift how an ambiguous score is written. Confidentiality alone cannot remove those pathways.
assumes: the trial team recruits, treats and measures while the trial runs
answerText: The board can see the arms because it is separated from recruitment, treatment and outcome scoring. Its knowledge can guide a recommendation without feeding back into the measurements still being made.

choices: It is separated from recruitment, treatment and outcome scoring
Its members are more qualified to interpret an early treatment difference
Its confidentiality rules prevent the result from affecting site behaviour
Its recommendation is advisory, so seeing the arms cannot influence the trial
rebuttals: Expertise helps the board interpret data, but expertise does not stop knowledge from changing measurements.
Confidentiality limits disclosure; it does not make knowledge harmless for people who recruit or score outcomes.
An advisory recommendation can change the trial. The protection comes from keeping the board outside data-producing roles.

why_this_format: The intellectual work is interpretation, not manipulation, so CHOICE is appropriate. The options were too easy because three distractors did not address the firewall between seeing data and changing data.

title: When the blind is opened for one person
task: Rule on a request to break one participant's code
scene: Diouf has a call from an intensive care registrar at three in the morning, on speaker. A CLARION-3 participant is in front of him and the treatment he is considering depends on what she has been receiving.
question: What makes this an occasion to open the code?
takeaway: The blind exists for the trial; it is opened when a decision for one person needs it.
why: A code break is judged on one question: is there a decision for this person, now, that turns on the answer? If there is, the blind loses and the participant wins, which is why the envelope exists and why nobody has to ask permission to open it. If there is not, then opening it takes a participant out of the analysis it belongs to and tells the site something it will not be able to unlearn. Every break is logged, and two in four years is the sort of number a well-run trial has.
assumes: each participant's assignment is held in a sealed record that can be opened

choices: Knowing the arm would change what the registrar does for her tonight
The participant has asked to know which arm she is on
The event is serious enough to be reported to the regulator
The trial is close to its interim and the case may be relevant to it
rebuttals: A participant's wish to know is taken seriously and is usually answered at the end of the trial.
Reportability is about what the regulator is told and does not require anybody at the site to know the arm.
Relevance to the interim is a reason for the board to look, not for the pharmacy to open an envelope.

dayTitle: The site that is faster than everybody
title: What a short screening log says
task: Choose the explanation that fits the whole screening log, not just the high entry rate.
scene: Thirty-one screening logs on one page. Most sites screen four and enter one. Site 12 screens eleven and enters nine, and its consent rate is the highest in the trial.
question: Which explanation best fits site 12's screening log?
takeaway: Recruitment figures describe a funnel, and an empty log hides the top of it.
why: The high entry rate is not the strongest clue. The nearly empty reasons column is. A site that truly screened eleven people and entered nine should still record why the other two were not entered. Across a year, it should also show many people who failed before consent. If those people never reach the log, the trial cannot describe who was considered and passed over. The result is a selected group whose recruitment funnel cannot be reconstructed.
assumes: sites record everybody they assess as well as everybody they enter
answerText: Site 12 appears to be logging people only after an informal pre-screen. That makes the visible funnel look unusually efficient because many people who were considered never appear at its top.

choices: The site is screening after it has already decided
The site is entering people who do not qualify
The site's population is genuinely more eligible
The site is unusually good at explaining the trial
rebuttals: Ineligible entries would appear as eligibility deviations, and none are recorded.
A more eligible catchment could raise the entry rate, but it would not empty the reasons column.
Better consent discussions could reduce refusals; they would not remove people who were assessed and found ineligible.
text.headline: Site 12 enters nine of every eleven people it logs as screened. Most sites enter about one in four.

why_this_format: The row has a headline and four candidates but no instrument panel. The intellectual move is selecting the explanation that fits the screening log, so it should render as CHOICE.

dayTitle: The site that is faster than everybody
title: Balance is bought in blocks
task: Check how the assignments have landed at site 12
scene: Diouf pulls site 12's kit records. The site has entered ninety-four participants, forty-nine to one arm and forty-five to the other, in a sequence that never runs more than four the same way.
question: Why is the sequence built so that no run of the same arm goes past four?
takeaway: Chance alone is unreliable in small numbers, which is why the sequence is constrained.
why: Pure chance is fine over two thousand people and unreliable over ninety. A site that closes at nineteen participants could easily have thirteen on one arm and six on the other, and any difference between sites then partly becomes a difference between arms. Working in small blocks forces the counts to catch up every few entries, so the arms are balanced within each site at every point. The cost is predictability, which is why the block length varies and why nobody at the site is told what it is.
assumes: assignment is by chance, in a sequence prepared before the trial opened

choices: It keeps the arms close in size at every site
It stops any site from receiving more of one treatment than another over the trial
It makes the next assignment harder for a coordinator to guess
It spreads the drug's supply evenly across the shipping schedule
rebuttals: Equal totals across the whole trial follow from balance at each site rather than being what blocking is for.
Blocking makes the sequence a little more guessable, not less; varying the block length is the fix.
Supply is planned from recruitment forecasts and does not drive the allocation sequence.

dayTitle: The site that is faster than everybody
title: Make the three-point offset move
task: Change one feature of the re-scoring setup at a time and find which change removes site 12's offset.
scene: Kwame Ansah has matched visit records from site 12 and three comparison sites. The symptom score sits about three points higher at site 12. A re-scoring console can change one feature of the setup for the same records.
question: Which single change makes the offset disappear, and does putting it back restore the offset?
takeaway: A suspected cause becomes persuasive when changing only that factor moves the reading and reversing it brings the effect back.
why: A site-wide offset can come from the patients, the timing of visits or the person applying the scale. The hard endpoint already argues against a healthier site 12 population. The control test goes further. It keeps the same records and changes one candidate cause at a time. Only the reader change moves the score by far more than the background noise. When the original reader is restored, the offset returns. That reversal is much stronger evidence than a correlation between site and score.
assumes: a systematic offset is a repeated shift rather than random scatter
a control test changes one factor while holding the rest fixed
answerText: Changing the reader removes the offset: it falls from about 3.0 points to 0.2, a 2.8-point shift. Restoring the site reader brings it back to about 3.1, while the other changes stay inside the noise threshold.

choices: How that site applies the scale, rather than how its patients are
That site 12's participants have milder disease than everybody else's
That the drug works better in site 12's population
That the scale is not sensitive enough to detect real differences
rebuttals: Milder disease would show up in the adjudicated events as well, and those match the other sites exactly.
A treatment effect would appear in one arm rather than shifting every score at the site.
An insensitive scale would blur differences rather than produce a steady offset at one site.

equations.about: absolute risk reduction — the difference the treatment made

why_this_format: The old multiple choice lets the player name 'the rater' without testing it. CONTROL makes them hold the records fixed, change one candidate cause, and confirm the result by reversal.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented test responses use the observed 3.0-point offset as the baseline. Noise is 0.5 point, so 3× noise is 1.5. Changing the reader moves the offset by 2.8 points and reversal restores 3.1; the other changes move it by only 0.1 and 0.3.

variables.label: Visit-day matching
variables.change: Match visits to the same study day

data.hint: Run one change at a time. Compare its shift with the 0.5-point noise, then put the changed factor back and run again.

failure_feedback.consequence: the score moves, but the run cannot identify which change caused it
failure_feedback.line: That gave us a difference. It did not give us a cause.

title: How much of the trial has happened
task: Work out how far through the trial really is
scene: Feldman has two numbers on the board: the events CLARION-3 was designed to need, and the events adjudicated so far. Balogun has a third, the months elapsed, and thinks it tells the same story.
question: Estimate the fraction of CLARION-3's information that is in hand today.
takeaway: The share of the planned events already collected is what says how far through a trial is.
why: Calendar time and information are different quantities, and only one of them decides what an interim can say. A trial three quarters of the way through its planned years may hold half its events, because the people recruited late have been followed for months rather than years and because a healthier group produces events more slowly. The boundary at each interim is set by the information fraction, not by the date, so a flattening event curve moves the meeting without moving the calendar. It is also why finishing takes longer than anyone forecasts.
assumes: the trial is powered on a number of events rather than a number of people
answerText: About 0.65 — roughly two thirds of the information.

estimate.prompt: CLARION-3 was designed to need 380 adjudicated events. The database holds 246 of them this morning. The information fraction is the events in hand divided by the events planned.
estimate.question: Choose the events collected and the events planned.
estimate.relationship: Information fraction = events observed ÷ events planned, and it is what fixes how hard an interim boundary has to be.
estimate.explanation: About two thirds. By months the trial looks three quarters done — 41 of 54 — and the two numbers disagree because the amendment brought in people at lower risk. The boundary the board reads in a fortnight is set from the 0.65, not from the calendar.

equations.about: information fraction — how far through an event-driven trial is
alpha spending — a budget for error that does not refill

title: Who a wider door lets in
task: Work out who the amendment brought in
scene: Marchetti has the entry criteria as they were and as they are, with the participants recruited under each. Balogun wants to know whether the amendment cost anything he should have seen coming.
question: Why has the event rate fallen since the amendment?
takeaway: Widening entry changes who is in the trial, and therefore how often the trial's event happens.
why: Entry criteria are a statement about risk. Loosening them admits people whose baseline chance of the event is lower, and a trial made of lower-risk people produces events more slowly whatever the drug does. Both arms are affected equally, so the comparison is still fair — but it takes longer to arrive, and a fixed number of events now needs more person-years to reach. Shorter follow-up on late recruits is real and separate, and it slows the count without changing who is in the trial.
assumes: entry criteria decide who may be randomised

choices: The trial now includes people at lower risk of the event
The drug has begun to work better than it did in the first years
Sites have become slower at reporting events to the database
Later participants have been followed for a shorter time each
rebuttals: A drug effect would separate the arms rather than lower the rate in both of them.
Reporting delays move events between months and do not reduce the total.
Shorter follow-up on recent recruits also slows the count, and it does not change the population.

equations.about: absolute risk reduction — the difference the treatment made

title: Changing the plan, on the record
task: Order what has to happen before a widened criterion may enrol anybody.
scene: Umeh has the amendment file open: the change, the approvals, the registry update and the date each happened. One of the four is a fortnight later than it should be.
takeaway: An amendment is judged by whether it was recorded before it was used, not by whether it was sensible.
why: The order is the protection. A change made for a stated reason, approved by people outside the trial, published before it is used and only then handed to sites, is a change nobody can have chosen after seeing what it would do to the results. Enrol first and register afterwards and there is no way, ever, to show the two were independent. The audit does not ask whether widening was wise — it asks whether the record was made before it mattered.
assumes: the entry criteria are part of the protocol and can be amended

cards: The change is drafted with the reason it is being made.
The ethics committee and the regulator approve the amended protocol.
The public registry entry is updated to the new criteria.
Sites are trained on the new criteria and begin using them.

title: Missing is not one thing
task: Match each gap to what it does to the comparison.
scene: Friday’s database lock is now on the wall clock. Four kinds of missing record are still in the queue, each with a count beside it. Renner wants one rule for all of them before the next site call starts.
takeaway: A gap that depends on what happened is not the same as a gap that does not.
why: Missing data are dangerous for different reasons. A missed visit because somebody moved is mostly a loss of precision. A missing outcome after a participant worsened is different, because the reason for the gap is tied to the thing being measured. That can bend the comparison. A form still sitting at a site is recoverable and should be chased before lock. Withdrawal of consent changes what the trial is allowed to pursue. One rule for every blank cell would hide these differences instead of managing them.
assumes: an outcome can be absent for reasons connected to the outcome itself

choices: Little: the reason has nothing to do with how they were doing.
A great deal: the sickest are disappearing, and possibly not evenly by arm.
Little, if the batch was whoever happened to be seen that week.
Unknown, and unknowable: nothing more may be collected about them.
scenarios: The participant moved abroad and left an address.
The participant stopped attending after their symptoms worsened.
The site's fax machine lost a batch of forms in March.
The participant withdrew consent and asked for no further contact.
columns: What it does to the comparison

equations.about: why precision improves only as the square root of the sample

title: Everyone as assigned
task: Choose which population the board is shown
scene: Two analyses are on Feldman's desk. One counts everybody in the arm they were assigned. The other counts only those who completed treatment, and it shows a bigger effect.
question: Why is the analysis by assigned arm the one the board is shown?
takeaway: Analysing people as assigned keeps the balance that randomisation bought.
why: Randomisation makes the arms alike in everything, including things nobody thought to measure. That balance belongs to the groups as assigned. The moment people are removed for something that happened afterwards — stopping the drug, missing visits, not completing — they are removed for a reason that is itself connected to how they were doing, and the two groups stop being comparable. The as-assigned analysis usually gives a smaller effect, and that is not a flaw in it: it is the effect of being offered the treatment, which is the decision a doctor actually faces.
assumes: some participants do not take the treatment they were assigned

choices: Dropping people who stopped treatment breaks the balance
It gives the larger and more convincing estimate of the effect
It is easier to compute from a database with missing fields in it
It counts every participant, so the trial keeps its statistical power
rebuttals: Analysing as assigned normally shrinks the estimate rather than enlarging it.
Both analyses are computable; the choice is about validity, not convenience.
Keeping everybody does preserve power, and power is not why the balance argument decides it.

title: Forty hours before the lock
task: Allocate the monitoring time so the required questions can still be answered before the file is frozen.
scene: Lucia Marchetti has a fortnight, thirty-one sites and forty monitoring hours she can still deploy. Four recoverable gaps compete for that time. Fourteen people who withdrew consent are locked out of the plan and cannot be contacted again.
question: Which monitoring jobs buy the answers the interim analysis actually needs?
takeaway: A monitoring plan is a set of questions it can answer and questions it deliberately leaves unanswered.
why: The dangerous gaps are not simply the largest ones. Forty-eight participants disappeared after worsening, so their missingness is tied to the outcome itself. That can bend the comparison if the losses differ by arm. Seven outcomes already exist on paper and are cheap to restore. People who moved are missing for a more neutral reason, so tracing them mainly improves precision. Rechecking complete records buys less. The allocation should protect validity first, then spend any remaining effort on precision.
assumes: missing outcomes are most dangerous when the reason for missingness is tied to the outcome
withdrawal of consent prevents further contact
answerText: Fund the 48 outcome-dependent losses and recover the seven paper forms. Those two jobs cost 34 of 40 hours and protect the questions the interim must answer; neutral losses and already-complete records can wait.

proposals: Trace the forty-eight who stopped attending after a worsening episode.
Recover the seven paper forms from the site that never faxed them.
Write again to the fourteen who withdrew consent.
Re-verify twenty completed records already in the database.
text.evidence: Ninety-one participants have no twelve-month outcome. Forty-eight of them stopped attending after a worsening episode was recorded — twenty-nine on one arm and nineteen on the other, though nobody blinded knows which arm is which. Twenty-two moved or emigrated. Fourteen withdrew consent. Seven are a lost batch of forms at one site, which the site still holds on paper.

why_this_format: The current ScienceTank describes scarce effort but never makes the player give anything up. ALLOCATE turns the fortnight into a finite pool and shows which analysis questions survive each spending plan.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented costs total 64 hours against a 40-hour pool. The two required answers need 28+6=34 hours. Buying the easy re-verification job first with the paper forms costs 18 and leaves only 22, which is not enough to trace the 48 outcome-dependent losses.

items.label: Trace 22 people who moved or emigrated

answers.label: Reduce outcome-dependent missingness before the cut
Restore outcomes already known to exist on paper
Reduce losses unrelated to health status
Repeat checks on records already complete

data.hint: The live panel shows which analysis questions your selected jobs can answer. You do not have enough hours to buy every job.

failure_feedback.action: funding easy re-verification before tracing the worsening group
failure_feedback.consequence: the remaining hours cannot cover the one missing-data problem that can bias the comparison
failure_feedback.line: Neat records are not the same thing as a safe comparison.

title: Kit that cannot be vouched for
task: Choose what the warm-storage excursion does to the comparison.
scene: Site 19 has already dispensed eleven boxes from the warm fridge to nine participants. Farida Diouf has the logger trace, dispensing list and stability sheets open. A replacement shipment will not reach the site until morning.
question: What is the most important effect of the site 19 excursion on the trial comparison?
takeaway: A storage failure damages one arm's material and leaves the other untouched.
why: Identical boxes can hide different contents. Heat can damage active drug, while the comparator has no active material to lose. The excursion can therefore pull treated participants toward the control result. That is different from an error that affects both arms equally. Eleven boxes are unlikely to change the whole trial, but the scale of the problem is a separate question from its direction. Recording the event lets later reviewers distinguish a small one-sided fault from a repeated one.
assumes: both arms receive kit that looks identical
answerText: The excursion can weaken active drug without weakening the comparator. That makes the error one-sided, even though eleven boxes in a four-thousand-box trial are unlikely to move the overall estimate much.

choices: It can weaken active drug without weakening the comparator
It should affect both arms equally because the boxes look identical
It invalidates every participant enrolled at site 19
It can be ignored because only eleven boxes were involved
rebuttals: Packaging can be identical while the contents respond differently to heat.
Excluding a whole site would discard unaffected participants and would not repair the exposed kits.
The small number limits the likely size of the effect; it does not make the deviation disappear.
text.headline: Eleven boxes spent forty-one hours above range at site 19. Nine participants received one of them.

why_this_format: There is no panel to diagnose. The row presents one headline and four explanations, so the existing interaction is a standard CHOICE.

title: What the nine are owed
task: Decide what the nine participants are told
scene: Nine people received kit from that fridge. Marchetti has to tell site 19 what to say to them, and Doyle has asked to see the wording before it goes.
question: What should the nine participants be told this week?
takeaway: A participant is owed what affects them, said in a way that does not tell them their arm.
why: Two duties pull in different directions and both can be met. People are entitled to know about a fault that touched their own treatment, and telling them costs the trial nothing if the wording covers all nine equally. Saying they may have been under-treated says the drug is in the box. Saying nothing because the arms are unknown treats the blind as more important than the person, which is the inversion the whole trial is arranged to avoid. Waiting for the board is twelve more days for information that is already certain.
assumes: participants are told about problems that affect their own treatment

choices: That a storage fault may have weakened some kit
Nothing, because the boxes cannot be linked to individual arms anyway
That they received kit from a faulty fridge and may have been under-treated
Nothing until the board has reviewed the excursion in twelve days
rebuttals: The link to arms is unknown, and the fault touched their treatment either way.
Telling somebody they were under-treated tells them which arm they are on.
The board reviews the excursion; it does not decide whether people hear about their own kit.

title: What the excursion record can actually prove
task: Use two verification checks on the claims in the excursion record before signing it as reviewable.
scene: Nkechi Umeh has the site 19 excursion form, the logger trace, dispensing records and an inventory statement. Four claims on the form are signed. She has time to verify only two before the deviation file closes.
question: Which claims most need verification before this record can support somebody else's judgement later?
takeaway: A signed record is useful only when the claims that could change the conclusion are tied to evidence.
why: A deviation form does not become reliable because somebody signed it. The duration can be checked against the logger, and the nine recipients can be checked against dispensing records. The important weak link is scope. If more than eleven kits were in the fridge, the size of the problem changes immediately. That claim needs an inventory reconciliation, not another signature. Recording the excursion still matters even if the final effect is small, because later reviewers can only challenge a judgement when its evidence survives.
assumes: a deviation record is evidence for later review
a signed statement records what someone asserts, not necessarily what the underlying records show
answerText: Verify the exposure scope and one of the backed critical claims. The weak point is the statement that only eleven kits were exposed; it needs stock reconciliation before the record can establish the excursion's true scope.

choices: Whether it mattered is a judgement others must be able to check
Regulators require every temperature reading to be filed
It protects the site from being blamed if the result is questioned
The kit has to be written off against the sponsor's supply budget
rebuttals: Loggers record continuously; what is filed is the departure and what was done about it.
Protection from blame is a by-product; the record exists for the analysis rather than the site.
Supply accounting happens anyway and is not what makes the entry a deviation.

why_this_format: The old choice asks why deviations are recorded. ATTEST makes the player test the stronger idea: a record is only reviewable when its critical claims can be checked against independent evidence.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented verification budget: there are four claims and only 2 checks. The 41-hour duration is critical and backed by the logger; the claim that only eleven kits were exposed is critical but unbacked until inventory is reconciled. At least one critical claim is backed and one is not.

claims.label: Only eleven kit numbers were exposed
claims.evidence: site inventory statement without stock reconciliation

claims.label: Nine participants received listed kits
claims.evidence: dispensing records linked to kit numbers

claims.label: The fridge returned to the allowed range

data.hint: A check opens the evidence behind one signed claim. Spend the two checks where a wrong claim would most change the size or meaning of the excursion.

failure_feedback.action: using both checks on already-backed minor details
failure_feedback.consequence: the record closes while the exposure scope still rests on an unsupported statement
failure_feedback.line: I can defend a conclusion only if I can defend what went into it.

title: The blind that had already gone
task: Choose the explanation that fits the guessing survey and the visible flush.
scene: At the annual visit, investigators and participants guessed each person's arm. Investigators were correct 71 per cent across 1,180 guesses. The case packet also contains first-fortnight symptom logs, the allocation audit and the adjudicated outcome summary.
question: What best explains investigators guessing the treatment arm correctly 71 per cent of the time?
takeaway: When a treatment announces itself, the people measuring stop being blind whatever the protocol says.
why: Seventy-one per cent correct across 1,180 guesses is far from the 50 per cent expected by chance. The visible flush also supplies a direct mechanism. Investigators can see it before they later score symptoms. A leaked allocation list could also raise guessing, but it would not explain participants guessing well too. Guessing from improvement would require a treatment effect much larger than the event data show. The survey therefore measures a real loss of blinding, not random noise.
assumes: blinding is meant to keep the person measuring from knowing the arm
answerText: The visible early flush is the best explanation. It gives investigators information about assignment before they later write the symptom score. The protocol may still say blinded while the measurement process is not.

choices: The visible early flush is revealing assignment
Someone has leaked the allocation list to investigators
Investigators are inferring assignment from dramatic clinical improvement
Seventy-one per cent is a plausible chance fluctuation in 1,180 guesses
rebuttals: A list leak could explain investigator guesses, but not why participants also guess above chance from the same early period.
The event data do not show an effect large enough to support that much accurate inference from improvement.
With 1,180 guesses, chance variation stays close to 50 per cent and cannot plausibly reach 71 per cent.
text.headline: Investigators guessed correctly 71 per cent of the time. Chance would be 50 per cent. First-fortnight logs show a visible flush concentrated in one arm.

why_this_format: The row has a headline and four explanations but no instrument panel. It is already a causal interpretation question, so CHOICE is the honest screen type.

title: Which measurements share the leak
task: Open each measurement's dependencies, keep the ones that do not inherit the blinding leak, and name the shared source.
scene: Feldman has four CLARION-3 measurements on the wall. The guessing survey says the blind has leaked. Each measurement came through a different path, and the sponsor wants to know which evidence still stands on its own.
question: Which measurements remain independent of the leak, and what source compromises the others?
takeaway: Agreement counts as independent evidence only when the measurements do not share the same route for bias to enter.
why: A blinding failure does not contaminate every number automatically. Bias needs a path. The treating clinician can see the flush, infer the arm and then write the symptom score. Participants can see the same flush and change how they take or return kit. The adjudication committee sees neither arm nor site, so that route is cut. The national death register is farther away still. Dependency tracing shows why four results pointing the same way are not automatically four independent pieces of evidence.
assumes: the visible flush can reveal treatment assignment
adjudication removes the arm and site before the committee rules
answerText: Keep the adjudicated admission and all-cause death as independent channels. The symptom score and returned-kit measure both have a path through the visible flush, which can reveal assignment before those measurements are produced.

choices: The symptom score, because the person who guessed also wrote it
The adjudicated event, because the committee reads files from unblinded sites
Both equally, because every measurement comes from the same participants
Neither, because the guessing survey is collected outside the analysis
rebuttals: The committee sees no arm and no site, so what the investigator believed cannot travel with the file.
Sharing participants does not share the route: the two outcomes are produced by different procedures.
The survey is collected outside the analysis and measures something that is inside it.

why_this_format: The old question asks the player to pick one damaged outcome. TRACE makes them inspect the dependency path for several measurements and distinguish shared bias from genuinely independent evidence.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Four channels are declared. Symptom score and kit return both depend on the visible flush, while adjudicated admission and death do not. Two channels share the target and two are independent. The admission rates are sourced from m10.s2; the symptom, adherence and death display readings are invented for this instrument because the stop sheet supplies no numeric values for them.

channels.label: Symptom score
channels.reading: Treatment-arm symptom scores average 3.4 points better than control.

channels.label: Returned-kit adherence
channels.reading: Returned-kit adherence is 89% in treatment and 84% in control.

data.hint: Open the dependency tree behind each measurement. Keep a channel only if its path does not pass through the source you think caused the blinding failure.

failure_feedback.action: discarding every measurement because the guessing survey failed
failure_feedback.consequence: independent channels are thrown away even though the blinding leak has no route into them
failure_feedback.line: A leak matters only where there is plumbing for it to travel through.

title: Telling the board what it does not yet know
task: Decide what has to enter tonight’s pack before the board sees the interim results.
scene: Vogt reads the interim pack in eleven days, and the PDF is queued for sign-off tonight. The guessing survey is absent because nobody expected it to matter. Balogun wants to leave it for the annual report.
question: What does the board most need in the pack because of the guessing survey?
takeaway: A board cannot weigh a result whose weakness it has not been shown.
why: The board has to see both evidence and the weaknesses attached to it. The guessing survey changes how the symptom score should be read, so leaving it out makes that score look cleaner than it is. The adjudicated endpoint still has a protected path and should remain separate. Stopping the whole trial would throw away evidence that survived the leak. Trying to re-blind people after a visible flush cannot repair measurements already made. The pack should show the problem and exactly which results it reaches.
assumes: the board decides whether the trial continues

choices: The survey, and the two outcomes reported separately
The survey, with a recommendation to stop the trial for unreliability
Nothing yet, since the survey does not change the adjudicated events
A plan to re-blind the trial by changing how the drug is given
rebuttals: The adjudicated events survive, and the board still has to be told which result is which.
Stopping discards a protected endpoint because a different one was damaged.
Changing administration now does nothing about the participants already assessed.

title: Reading the same files twice
task: Check the committee's re-read for the thing it could still get wrong
scene: The committee has re-read four hundred files. Ansah is asked whether a second reading by the same three people, who now know a guessing survey exists, can be trusted at all.
question: What keeps the second reading from drifting?
takeaway: Consistency between two readings comes from the rule, not from memory.
why: A second reading is useful only if it is anchored to the same rule as the first. Memory is not enough, especially after readers learn that blinding may have failed elsewhere. The committee therefore reopens the written definition, not the previous verdict. Borderline files are scored against explicit criteria and disagreements are recorded. If the second pass moves only because readers now expect a problem, that is drift. If it moves because the same rule is applied more consistently, the change is evidence about the original measurement process.
assumes: the adjudication committee never sees the arm

choices: The definition was agreed before any file was read
The readers do not remember their first rulings
Each file is read by a different member the second time
The committee is told the trial's overall result first
rebuttals: Readers remember hard cases, which is why the definition rather than forgetting is the safeguard.
Rotating readers helps consistency and does not stop a shared definition from being applied loosely.
Telling the committee the overall result is precisely what would let a ruling drift toward it.

title: How big, and how wide
task: Translate the effect into NNT, then put a number on the sampling noise behind one arm rate.
scene: The press office has lifted “4.2 percentage points” into a draft briefing. Feldman circles the interval beside it. Before the number leaves the room, she wants the team to put both clinical size and sampling noise on the result.
question: Estimate the NNT, then estimate the standard error of the 18.9 per cent control-arm event rate.
takeaway: Effect size says how large the difference is; standard error says how much the estimate would move across repeated samples.
why: The risk difference and NNT describe the size of the observed benefit. Precision is a different question. For a proportion, standard error depends on both the event rate and the number measured. With about 1,200 people in the control arm, an 18.9 per cent rate has an SE near 1.1 percentage points. A 95 per cent margin is about twice that. Increasing the sample narrows this uncertainty only with the square root of n, so halving the SE takes about four times as many people.
assumes: the 2,400 participants are allocated about equally between two arms
a proportion estimated from a sample has sampling error
answerText: About 24 people treated for one event avoided; the control-arm event rate has SE ≈ 0.011, or 1.1 percentage points.

estimate.prompt: The adjudicated event happened in 18.9 per cent of control and 14.7 per cent of treatment, with about 1,200 people per arm. First use ARR = p_control − p_treatment and NNT = 1/ARR. Then use SE = √(p(1−p)/n) for the control rate and 1.96 × SE for a 95 per cent margin.
estimate.question: Choose the two event rates and the approximate number in one arm.
estimate.relationship: ARR = p_control − p_treatment; NNT = 1/ARR; SE = √(p(1−p)/n); a 95% margin is about 1.96 × SE.
estimate.explanation: NNT is about 24. The control-arm SE is about 0.011, or 1.1 percentage points, so its 95 per cent margin is about 2.2 points. The first number describes clinical size; the second describes sampling precision. Halving that SE would require about four times the sample, not twice.
givens: Control arm event rate 18.9 per cent
Treatment arm event rate 14.7 per cent
labels: 0.95  (a tempting probability, but not an input to either calculation)

equations.about: absolute risk reduction — the difference the treatment made
number needed to treat, and why it is the honest headline
why precision improves only as the square root of the sample
a confidence interval, and what its width says

title: What to do about a blind that leaks
task: Decide what to do about the blind for everybody still enrolling
scene: Six hundred participants are still in follow-up and the flush has not stopped happening. Diouf has been asked whether there is anything the pharmacy can do about it at this stage.
question: What is the best available fix for the remaining follow-up?
takeaway: When a treatment cannot be hidden, protect the measurement instead of pretending the blind holds.
why: The blind has already failed for anybody who saw the first fortnight, and nothing recovers it for them. What can still be protected is the route from belief into the number: separate the assessor from the treating team, and the score is written by somebody with nothing to infer from. Matching the comparator's appearance is the right design and it is four years too late to introduce here. Leaving it in the notes matters — the notes are the source record — and a limitation paragraph fixes nothing while six hundred people are still being scored.
assumes: the drug produces an early visible effect that the comparator does not

choices: Scoring by someone who never sees the early visits
Add a substance to the comparator so it produces a similar flush
Ask investigators to stop recording the flush in the notes
Accept the leak and note it as a limitation in the final paper
rebuttals: Changing the comparator mid-trial creates two different control arms and cannot be applied backwards.
The flush is a clinical finding; leaving it out of the notes damages the record and hides nothing from the treating doctor.
A limitation in the paper describes the problem for readers and does nothing for the scores still being written.

title: Freezing something that was moving
task: Say what the lock protects, and what kind of problem could justify breaking it.
scene: The database-lock checklist is projected on the wall and the cut is three days away. Umeh has one question from the sponsor and another from Renner: once the file freezes, what exactly would justify opening it again?
question: What does locking the database buy the interim analysis?
takeaway: Locking fixes what the analysis was run on, so the result can be checked later.
why: A database lock creates a version of the trial that cannot quietly move under the analysis. Queries are closed, coding is fixed and the dataset is frozen before the planned calculation runs. That makes the result reproducible later. Reopening is possible, but it must be exceptional and documented because it creates a new version of the evidence. A discovered error that changes a primary event can justify that step. A cosmetic correction usually cannot. The point is not permanence; it is a visible boundary around what the analysis actually used.
assumes: data arrive from sites continuously while a trial runs

choices: A fixed dataset that anybody can rerun the analysis on
A guarantee that the data contain no remaining errors
Protection from sites amending records they have already sent
A point after which the trial no longer collects information
rebuttals: Errors that nobody has found are locked in with everything else; the lock is about repeatability.
Sites keep working and keep correcting; later changes go into the next locked version.
Collection continues after the lock, which is why the next analysis has a different cut.

title: Three days, forty-one queries
task: Keep the one query that cannot miss Thursday's cut and delegate the others with an owner, first action and return condition.
scene: Forty-one queries remain and the interim file locks in three working days. One concerns a primary-event date, one a duplicated visit, and thirty-nine are contact-field corrections. Renner has two people available, and you can keep only one problem yourself.
question: What do you keep, what do you hand off, and what must each delegated owner bring back?
takeaway: Urgency belongs to the problem whose consequence becomes irreversible first, not to the problem making the most noise.
why: The biggest pile is not the most urgent problem. A missing event date can decide whether a primary event exists in Thursday's analysis at all. Once the file is cut, that omission cannot be repaired for this interim. The duplicate visit is important but stable, and a site monitor can reconcile it against the source note. Contact-field corrections are numerous and visible, yet they do not change the endpoint count. Good delegation protects the irreversible decision while giving stable work clear owners and return rules.
assumes: an event outside the cut is absent from this interim analysis
delegation needs an owner, a first action and a condition for returning the problem
answerText: Keep the primary-event date because Thursday makes its consequence irreversible. Delegate the duplicate visit for source reconciliation and batch the contact corrections, with a return condition only if they begin blocking follow-up.

choices: A participant's event date, which decides whether it falls inside the window
A misspelled hospital name on four consent records
A missing telephone number on the contact sheet
A visit recorded twice in the same week at one site
rebuttals: A misspelling belongs in the record and cannot move an endpoint either way.
The contact sheet matters for follow-up rather than for what is counted at the cut.
A duplicated visit is worth resolving and is not an event on its own.

why_this_format: The existing triage screen can rank queries but cannot teach ownership. DELEGATE forces the player to protect the irreversible event-date problem while giving the other work a real first move and return condition.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Exactly one problem is rising and irreversible: the event date can miss a cut only 3 working days away, while resolution can consume 1–2 days. The duplicate is stable. The contact pile is loud and grows by an invented 5 per day, but it has no Thursday analysis deadline. Rate details beyond the three-day cut and 41-query total are invented for the DELEGATE board.

problems.label: Primary-event date unresolved
problems.consequence: If it is unresolved at the cut, the event is absent from this interim.
problems.rate: 3 working days to Thursday cut; source retrieval and site confirmation can consume 1–2 working days.

problems.label: Visit appears twice in one week
problems.consequence: A visit-level measure could be duplicated until the source note is checked.
problems.rate: 1 duplicated visit is open; no second duplicate has appeared in the last 6 working days.

problems.label: Large pile of contact-field corrections
problems.consequence: Follow-up administration stays messy, but Thursday's endpoint count does not change.
problems.rate: 39 contact-field corrections are open and about 5 more arrive per day; they have no Thursday analysis deadline.

firstActions.label: Pull the admission and discharge source record
Compare both visit entries with the signed site note
Return the contact list to sites as one batch

returnConditions.label: Return when the event date is documented or shown unknowable
Return when one or both visit entries are confirmed against source
Return only if a missing field blocks scheduled participant follow-up

data.hint: Keep one problem yourself. Every delegated problem needs an owner, a first action and a condition that tells the owner when it comes back to you.

failure_feedback.consequence: the only irreversible query reaches the cut without an owner or a first action
failure_feedback.line: If it can vanish from Thursday's analysis, 'watch it' is not a plan.

title: Nothing left in the tray
task: Decide what the committee still owes before the lock
scene: Ansah has nineteen files still under adjudication and three days. Two of the nineteen are from participants recruited in the first year and have been waiting on one missing discharge summary each.
question: Why must the committee clear its tray before the file is locked?
takeaway: An unadjudicated event is invisible to the analysis, whatever the notes say.
why: Adjudication is not paperwork after the fact; it is the step that turns something that happened into a countable event. Nineteen files sitting in a tray are nineteen events the analysis will behave as though nobody had. That is not neutral: files wait longest where the evidence is thinnest, and the thin files are not evenly spread between arms. Rulings made after the lock go into the next version, which means the interim was read on a trial that was quietly missing part of itself.
assumes: an event is only counted once the committee has ruled on it

choices: Events without a ruling are absent from the analysis
A ruling made after the lock cannot be entered into any database
The committee's rulings determine which arm each participant is in
Unadjudicated files count as missing outcomes for those participants
rebuttals: Later rulings are entered normally; they simply arrive after this analysis has been run.
The committee rules on events and never sees or determines the arm.
The participant is not missing; one of their events is uncounted, which is a different fault.

title: The subgroup that crossed
task: Say what a subgroup crossing its line is worth
scene: Participants over seventy show a difference that clears the line on its own. Feldman asks which of fourteen prespecified subgroups this is, and whether anybody has looked at the other thirteen yet.
question: What is the first thing to establish about the over-seventies result?
takeaway: A subgroup result is one of many results, and it has to be judged as one of many.
why: Every subgroup is another test. Test enough of them and one will look impressive whatever the drug does. Fourteen slices at the usual threshold give better than even odds that at least one clears the line by luck. So the count comes first. It decides what the result means, before anybody argues about mechanism. Group size matters. So does the direction of the other slices, and so does the biology. All three are read differently once you know whether this was the only question asked, or the fourteenth.
assumes: a subgroup is a slice of the participants analysed on its own

choices: How many subgroups were examined
Whether the biology makes sense in older participants
Whether the other thirteen subgroups point the same way
How large the over-seventy group is
rebuttals: Plausibility can be constructed for almost any subgroup after the fact, which is why it is not first.
Consistency across slices is genuine evidence, and it means little until the number of looks is known.
Size matters for precision and does not say how many chances the result had to appear.

equations.e: P(at least one false positive) = 1 − (1 − α)^k
equations.about: multiplicity — what testing k things costs

title: The update that is due Friday
task: Assemble the safety update the regulator has asked for
scene: The regulator wants the liver cases written up by Friday. There are now four, not two. Vogt has seen all four by arm; nobody else in the building has.
question: What must Friday's update contain to be worth reading?
takeaway: A safety update reports the events and the denominator, not a conclusion about them.
why: Four cases do not say how common the problem is. Four cases among forty exposed people mean something very different from four among twelve hundred. The regulator needs both the numerator and denominator, plus enough clinical detail to recognise a pattern. Causality opinions can be included, but they do not replace the counts. Efficacy results belong to the board's closed review. A recommendation about continuing also comes later, after the people responsible for that decision have the same safety evidence.
assumes: serious events are reported to regulators on a stated schedule
answerText: The update needs the four cases, the number of people exposed, and enough timing and clinical detail to understand the pattern. A case count without its denominator is not a rate.

choices: The four cases, the exposed population, and the timing and clinical pattern
The four cases, the board's current causality judgement, and no exposure denominator
The four cases beside the interim efficacy estimate and treatment-arm difference
The four cases with a recommendation on whether recruitment should continue
rebuttals: A causality view can accompany the report, but without the exposed population the reader cannot interpret frequency.
The interim efficacy result belongs to the board's protected review and is not needed to make the safety update interpretable.
A continuation recommendation is a decision built from the evidence, not a substitute for reporting the evidence itself.

why_this_format: This remains a reporting judgement, so CHOICE is appropriate. The original keyed option was noticeably shorter and more obviously factual than the three policy distractors.

title: What the Lyon paper is worth tonight
task: Spend tonight's review budget on the parts of the Lyon result that could change what CLARION-3 asks its board to consider.
scene: The Lyon trial published a large benefit at 6:10 this morning. By lunch, Balogun wants CLARION-3 to respond. Nkechi Umeh has the paper, its supplement and four review hours before she must state the trial’s position.
question: Which pieces of the Lyon evidence are worth buying before tonight's position is written?
takeaway: External evidence matters in proportion to how much it can change the decision, not how dramatic its headline sounds.
why: A striking outside result is neither ignored nor copied into the current trial. First ask whether it measured the same kind of outcome, on enough events, with uncertainty narrow enough to matter. Then ask whether its randomisation protected the comparison. Those features determine how much the paper should change the board's uncertainty. A plausible mechanism or an impressive subgroup can support interpretation, but they cannot rescue an incomparable endpoint. The result belongs in the board's discussion, while CLARION-3's registered analysis remains fixed.
assumes: a related trial can change the uncertainty that makes continued randomisation defensible
an outside result does not rewrite a prespecified analysis plan
answerText: Read the endpoint definition, event count and confidence interval first, then the randomisation methods if time remains. Those tell you whether Lyon is both comparable and credible enough to change what the board weighs; the analysis plan itself stays unchanged.

choices: What the board is asked to consider at the interim
The trial's analysis plan, updated to match Lyon's endpoint
Recruitment, which stops until the paper has been reviewed
Nothing, since it studied a different drug
rebuttals: Rewriting the plan to match a published endpoint destroys the claim that it was chosen in advance.
Suspending recruitment acts on evidence nobody blinded has weighed against the trial's own.
A related drug in a smaller trial is relevant evidence rather than none.

why_this_format: The original choice has one policy answer. VALUE makes the player decide which parts of an external result deserve scarce review time before deciding how strongly it should enter the board's deliberation.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented review costs total 9 hours against a 4-hour budget. Endpoint comparability costs 2 hours and is decisive. Buying the press release plus biological commentary costs 3 hours and leaves only 1, so the decisive endpoint check can no longer be bought.

title: How often something clears the line by luck
task: Put a number on fourteen looks
scene: Fourteen prespecified subgroups, each tested at the usual five per cent. Feldman writes the arithmetic on the board and asks what the chance is that at least one clears the line with no real difference anywhere.
question: Estimate the chance that at least one of fourteen subgroups clears the line by luck alone.
takeaway: The chance of at least one false positive rises fast with the number of tests.
why: Each test carries its own small chance of being wrong, and the chances do not stay small when they are stacked. With independent tests the probability that none misfires is 0.95 multiplied by itself once per test, so fourteen tests leave barely half the outcomes clean. That is the arithmetic behind every impressive subgroup: not that anybody cheated, but that a room looking in fourteen places will usually find something in one of them. Real subgroups overlap and correlate, which softens the number without changing the lesson.
assumes: each test has a five per cent chance of a false positive on its own
answerText: About 51 per cent — near enough a coin toss.

estimate.prompt: Fourteen subgroups are each tested at a five per cent level. If nothing is really different anywhere, the chance that none of them clears the line is 0.95 raised to the fourteenth power. The chance that at least one does is one minus that.
estimate.question: Choose the per-test pass rate and the number of tests.
estimate.relationship: Chance of at least one false positive = 1 − (1 − α)^m, with α the level of each test and m the number of tests.
estimate.explanation: About one in two. Fourteen honest looks at a trial where the treatment does the same thing in everybody will produce at least one subgroup clearing the line about half the time, which is why the over-seventies finding is not evidence on its own.
givens: Each is tested at the five per cent level

equations.e: P(at least one false positive) = 1 − (1 − α)^k
equations.about: multiplicity — what testing k things costs

title: The slice, and what it was scored on
task: Check what the over-seventies analysis actually measured
scene: The over-seventies result is on the symptom score rather than the adjudicated event. Ansah points out that this is the outcome the guessing survey landed on, and that older participants attend most often.
question: What does the over-seventies result rest on?
takeaway: A subgroup finding inherits every weakness of the outcome it was measured with.
why: Two weaknesses compound here. The finding is one of fourteen subgroup looks, so chance already has many opportunities to produce something interesting. It is also measured on the symptom score, which the guessing survey showed can inherit treatment knowledge. Older participants attend more often, creating more scored visits where a small bias can enter. The adjudicated event in the same subgroup shows nothing unusual. That contrast matters: the subgroup signal is strongest exactly where the measurement process is least protected.
assumes: the symptom score is written by the treating doctor and the event is adjudicated

choices: The outcome the unblinding was shown to reach
The adjudicated endpoint, in a smaller group
A separate scale used only in older participants
The same endpoint, scored by the committee twice
rebuttals: The adjudicated endpoint shows nothing unusual in this slice, which is what makes the contrast informative.
No separate scale exists for older participants; the same instrument is used throughout.
The committee's second reading covered ambiguous files across the trial, not this subgroup.

title: What to say about a slice
task: Write what the board is told about the subgroup
scene: Vogt will see the over-seventies table whatever the pack says about it. What the pack can do is tell her what she is looking at before she looks at it.
question: How should the over-seventies table be presented to the board?
takeaway: A subgroup table is reported with the number of looks that produced it.
why: A single striking slice on its own page invites the reader to treat it as the finding. The same slice as the eleventh row of fourteen invites them to count, which is the right reaction. Presenting all of them costs nothing and removes the choice of what to emphasise from whoever assembles the pack. Leaving it out is worse than either: the board is the body entitled to see everything, and a pack that filters what looks unlikely has started making the board's decision for it.
assumes: the board sees the trial's subgroup tables in closed session

choices: Beside all fourteen subgroups, on the same page
On its own, with the biological argument for it
Left out, since it is unlikely to be real
First, because it is the strongest signal in the pack
rebuttals: A biological argument beside one slice makes it look chosen for its plausibility rather than found among many.
Withholding a table decides for the board what it is allowed to weigh.
Ordering the pack by how strong something looks is the emphasis the board is meant to supply.
