title: Three things the board can say
task: Match each recommendation to what the board gives up by making it.
scene: Vogt’s board meets behind a closed door in forty minutes. The adjudicated effect is modest, the stopping boundary is not crossed, and four liver cases remain unexplained. Three recommendations are printed on separate cards in front of her.
takeaway: Each way of ending a trial buys something and gives something up.
why: None of the board’s three choices is free. Stopping for benefit before the boundary is crossed risks exaggerating an effect and loses future safety follow-up. Stopping for futility can discard a modest benefit that more events might confirm. Continuing preserves the planned evidence but keeps people exposed to the arm doing worse so far. Even changing what gets reported has a cost. The registered plan is part of why readers can trust the result, so any change has to be recorded before it is used.
assumes: a monitoring board recommends and the sponsor decides

choices: The long-term safety data, and a precise estimate — early stops overstate effects.
A modest but real benefit, which the trial would have gone on to confirm.
Another year in which half of those recruited receive the arm that loses.
Comparability with the plan as registered, unless the change is recorded first.
scenarios: Stop now for benefit, on an effect that has not crossed the boundary.
Stop now for futility, on the grounds that the effect is small.
Continue to the planned number of events.
Continue, with the symptom score dropped from the primary reporting.

equations.about: information fraction — how far through an event-driven trial is

equations.e: conditional power = P(significant at the end | data so far)
equations.about: what a futility forecast is, and what it is not

title: What the rest of the trial would probably do
task: Say how likely the trial is to finish positive
scene: Feldman has computed what the trial would most likely conclude if it ran to 380 events, given the 246 in hand. Balogun asks the obvious question: if it is going to end positive, why wait.
question: What does a conditional power of 78 per cent tell the board?
takeaway: A forecast about a study is not a statement about the treatment.
why: Conditional power forecasts the trial under an assumption about what happens next. It starts with the data already collected and asks how often the final test would cross its line if the remaining events behave as assumed. A value of 78 per cent argues against stopping for futility. It does not say there is a 78 per cent chance the treatment works. It also does not say the current result is significant. The stopping boundary answers that separate question.
assumes: the trial has collected about two thirds of its planned events
answerText: A conditional power of 78 per cent is a forecast under an assumption about the remaining data. About 78 per cent of comparable continuations would finish significant. It is not the probability that the treatment works.

choices: Under the stated future-data assumption, about 78 per cent of comparable continuations would finish significant
Given the current data, the probability that the treatment truly has a benefit is 78 per cent
Seventy-eight per cent of the information needed for the final analysis has already been collected
The current interim result has a 78 per cent chance of crossing today's stopping boundary
rebuttals: That would be a probability about the treatment itself and requires a different framework and assumptions.
Information fraction is events observed divided by events planned; here it is about two thirds.
Today's boundary is evaluated with today's statistic. Conditional power forecasts a future final analysis.

equations.about: how many events a trial has to see to answer its question

equations.e: conditional power = P(significant at the end | data so far)
equations.about: what a futility forecast is, and what it is not

why_this_format: Conditional power is an interpretation problem, and a short CHOICE screen is better than an instrument here. The keyed option originally paraphrased the question so closely that it could be selected without understanding the conditioning assumption.

title: What a stop obliges
task: Order what has to happen if the board recommends stopping tomorrow.
scene: Umeh has the registry entry, protocol and publication policy open before the board call. One participant is due an infusion on Monday. Doyle asks what happens, in what order, if the board recommends stopping tomorrow.
takeaway: Ending recruitment does not end the trial's obligations to the people in it.
why: A stop is an event with a sequence, and the sequence is about who learns what and when. The sponsor decides, because the board only recommends. Sites and participants come next and quickly: somebody is due an infusion on Monday and is entitled to know. The public record is corrected because a registered trial that quietly disappears is how the literature acquires missing arms. And reporting is not optional — a trial stopped early still owes its results, with the shortened follow-up stated plainly.
assumes: a trial's commitments continue after recruitment ends

cards: The sponsor accepts the recommendation and sets a date recruitment ends.
Sites are told, and participants already enrolled are told what changes for them.
The registry entry is updated to say the trial stopped and why.
The results are reported, including the follow-up that was cut short.

title: One relative risk, many absolute effects
task: Move the two event rates until they reproduce the reported relative risk, then use the absolute risk reduction to collapse the possibilities.
scene: Two lines for the board chair’s closed briefing describe the same CLARION-3 result. One says risk fell about 22 per cent; the other says roughly four events were prevented per hundred people. Umeh puts both arm rates on a two-control display.
question: How many pairs of arm risks fit the relative result, and what second measurement identifies the CLARION-3 pair?
takeaway: A relative effect does not determine the absolute benefit until the baseline risk is known.
why: A ratio does not carry the baseline rate with it. Treatment and control risks of 3.9 and 5 per cent give almost the same relative reduction as 14.7 and 18.9 per cent. The absolute benefits are very different. That is why the relative result forms a whole line of possible pairs on the display. Adding the measured absolute reduction gives a second line. Their intersection recovers the actual arm rates and shows why an absolute statement carries information the relative headline leaves out.
assumes: relative risk is treatment risk divided by control risk
absolute risk reduction is control risk minus treatment risk
answerText: The relative risk alone allows many pairs. Adding ARR = 0.042 selects the CLARION-3 rates: 0.189 in control and 0.147 in treatment. Their ratio is about 0.778, a 22 per cent relative reduction.

choices: It states the reduction as a share of the control risk
It uses a larger and more recent dataset than Feldman's
It includes the subgroup where the effect was largest
It rounds the estimate towards the top of the interval
rebuttals: Both sentences use the same locked dataset and the same analysis.
The subgroup is not in either sentence; the sponsor's uses the whole trial.
Neither rounds to the interval's edge; the difference is which denominator is used.

why_this_format: The old choice says the relative form uses a denominator. DEGENERACY lets the player discover that many control and treatment risks produce the same relative risk, then watch the absolute difference select the actual pair.
trap_is_satisfied_by: The RR≈0.778 locus has five separated pairs. With tolerances of 0.010 on p_control and 0.008 on p_treatment, the four non-truth pairs lie outside the answer window. The ARR=0.042 locus crosses the RR locus at p_control=0.189 and p_treatment=0.147, so the second measurement collapses the family to the CLARION-3 pair.

data.hint: First match the relative risk. Notice how many rate pairs work. Then reveal the absolute reduction and find where the two constraint lines cross.

failure_feedback.action: stopping after matching the 0.778 relative risk
failure_feedback.consequence: many very different baseline risks remain equally compatible with the headline
failure_feedback.line: You matched the ratio. You still have not told me how many people benefit.

title: What can be claimed
task: State what the trial has established about its endpoint
scene: Ansah is asked to write one sentence about the adjudicated endpoint for the board's minutes. He has the effect, the interval, and the fact that the trial has not finished.
question: Which sentence does CLARION-3's adjudicated endpoint currently support?
takeaway: An honest claim carries its uncertainty and the conditions it was measured under.
why: An interim estimate is evidence, but it is not the final word. The point estimate says where the observed difference sits, and the interval shows the range still compatible with the data. More events can move both. Saying there is no effect until the target event count is reached throws away information already collected. Claiming the effect is specific to older participants imports a fragile subgroup result. Claiming the trial should have stopped ignores the stopping boundary the board actually used.
assumes: the interval around an estimate says what the data are compatible with
answerText: The current data support an effect of about four percentage points on the adjudicated endpoint. There is uncertainty around that estimate, and more events are still to come.

choices: The adjudicated endpoint currently differs by about four points, with uncertainty and further follow-up still ahead
The primary endpoint cannot support any effect statement until all 380 planned events have occurred
The four-point effect is established most clearly in participants over seventy because that subgroup crossed its own line
The four-point effect is already strong enough to justify stopping because the interval excludes no effect
rebuttals: Interim data already contain information; the final event count determines precision and the planned stopping rule, not whether the current estimate exists.
That subgroup was one of fourteen and was strongest on the outcome most exposed to the blinding failure.
Statistical evidence against no effect is not identical to crossing the prespecified early-stopping boundary.

title: What happens to the people in it
task: Write the rule for what sites tell participants after the board says continue.
scene: The board has said continue. At eight Monday morning, thirty-one sites will open their phones and 2,400 participants will still be enrolled. Marchetti has one letter to tell every site what changes, and what does not.
question: What are the participants owed now that the board has reported?
takeaway: Consent is maintained, not collected once.
why: Consent is a continuing decision, not a signature stored from four years ago. Participants should know facts that could reasonably affect whether they stay. Here the safe fact is that an independent board reviewed the trial and recommended continuing. Releasing the unblinded interim numbers would let treatment knowledge spread back through participants and sites. Telling somebody their own arm would do the same. Saying nothing also fails the obligation, because a meaningful review happened. The update should preserve both informed participation and the comparison still under way.
assumes: participants continue treatment and follow-up until the trial ends

choices: That the trial reviewed its data and is continuing, and why
The interim result, so they can decide whether to stay
Nothing, since nothing about their treatment changes
Their own arm, now that an interim analysis has been done
rebuttals: Releasing the interim result to participants unblinds the trial by another route.
Silence leaves people unaware that a review happened at all.
Telling somebody their arm removes them from the comparison they consented to be part of.
